fixes.answer: There are several compelling reasons. Studying abroad often provides access to higher-quality education and internationally recognised qualifications, which boost career prospects. Beyond academics, it offers an invaluable chance to experience a new culture, gain independence and [[broaden one's horizons]]. For many, it is a genuinely [[transformative]] personal journey as much as an academic one, offering [[exposure]] that home study cannot match.
fixes.why: marked the full phrase 'broaden one's horizons'

fixes.answer: It depends entirely on the individual and their goals. Studying abroad offers [[cultural immersion]] and independence that home study cannot, and sometimes access to better facilities. However, it is expensive, and studying at home is cheaper, closer to family, and free of the challenge of adapting to a foreign culture. So neither is universally better; it is a matter of [[weighing]] the [[enrichment]] against the cost and difficulty.
fixes.why: 'adapting' and 'cost' are plain; marked 'cultural immersion' and 'weighing'

fixes.answer: They face numerous challenges. Culture shock and homesickness are extremely common, especially at first. A language barrier can make both study and daily life difficult and [[isolating]]. There are also practical hurdles, like managing finances and navigating an unfamiliar system alone. Adapting to different academic expectations can be [[daunting]] too. However, overcoming these difficulties is precisely what makes the experience so rewarding and [[character-building]].

The benefits can be substantial. Students who return bring back advanced knowledge, new skills and valuable international perspectives that can drive innovation and development at home. They also form global networks that can [[foster]] trade and collaboration. However, there is a risk of a brain drain if graduates choose to stay abroad. So the benefit to the home country depends heavily on [[repatriating]] that talent and [[expertise]].

I think physical study abroad will remain popular but may face competition from online alternatives. Increasingly, students can access foreign universities' courses remotely, offering the academic benefits without the cost of [[relocating]]. However, the cultural and personal growth of actually living abroad is [[irreplaceable]], so demand will [[persist]]. The future may see a mix of physical and virtual international education, making it more accessible and diverse.

The advantages are significant: exposure to a new culture, greater independence, improved language skills, and often a superior education, all of which boost [[employability]]. The disadvantages, however, include the high financial cost, the [[emotional strain]] of homesickness, and the difficulty of adjusting to an unfamiliar environment. So it offers immense personal and academic growth, but [[at a considerable price]] in both money and comfort.
fixes.why: 'adjusting', 'growth', 'price' are plain; marked 'employability', 'emotional strain', 'at a considerable price'

fixes.answer: I broadly agree, provided there are sensible conditions. Funding talented students to gain world-class education and skills abroad can be a smart investment in a country's future development. However, to avoid a [[brain drain]], such funding could reasonably require graduates to return and contribute for a period. So I support it as a [[strategic investment]], as long as the country actually [[reaps]] the eventual benefits of that investment.
fixes.why: 'benefits' and 'investment' are plain; marked 'brain drain' and 'strategic investment'
